title: Vermont Data Collaborative Data Engineering 101 and Assignment
text:
Getting Started
As you work through this and the following sections, please number your responses the same. You can do this with subsections “## 1” or with a list of numbers as I have done.

Create a new .qmd in your repository titled VDC-Data-Engineering.qmd and make sure that the render name is prettier. Start a first section: “# Getting Started”
Go to our main github page. This is the repo you’ll largely be working on for the next month.
Navigate to the README step 1 in the “installation and setup” section to get the project locally installed on your computer, do the following steps. Do not skip the large file storage part.

NOTE: these steps are built around an assumption that you know how to use your computers terminal. If you don’t know how to do that, find a tutorial online or ask AI to help you get some baseline skills.

Read through the Vision.md and Codebase_Primer.md files in the Design/current folder locally. Take notes and write down questions in your .qmd file. As you move through the codebase file, quickly scan the files in the folders it covers and get a rough sense of how they work.
Complete the rest of the github’s README instructions. Troubleshoot and ask questions until you have a local version of the website that you can click through on your computer. Note any areas of particular difficulty or possibilities for improvement in your .qmd.
Look at the filter on the zoning exploratory mapping page. Does the idea of a cascading filter make sense to you? Write an explanation in your qmd.
If you’re using VSCODE, I recommend installing the following extensions and briefly reading their readmes.

quarto
inline sql
quack syntax




Getting Familiar

Start a new section in your .qmd: “# Getting Familiar”
Read through backend/app_utils/zoning.py, the deprecated code for runtime cleaning and adjustments on the zoning atlas data.

Make sure that you follow function definitions (F12 in VS Code is a useful hotkey for this).
Write an explanation of how the tooltips are generated in your .qmd, both in the abstract and for zoning in particular. Either speculate, or look at the frontend code to get a sense of how the tooltip might be shown to the user.
Take notes and write down questions in your .qmd.

Read through design/current/Data_Engineering.md in the same folder.

Take notes and write down questions in your .qmd.
Read sections 1-3 of the linked Tidy Data article closely.

Summarize the article.
Skim the rest of it, if interested.

Explain the referenced schema.json. If you don’t know about .json files, read and watch youtube videos about them, etc., for at least an hour.
Explain how the filters work.

Where is information about them stored?
What is the difference between the primary dataset and secondary dataset keys?
I want to filter a zoning query that selects all zoning areas that are designated for Affordable Housing with a spatial intersection of census areas that have a population over 10.000 (note, census is not yet in the schema.json).

What is my primary dataset?
What is my secondary dataset?
What is my join_key?
What is my join_type?
Speculate as to what the columns might be, or look through the census tables to find out what columns might make sense for such a filter.



Read through backend/notebooks/zoning/table_build.qmd. Take notes and write down questions in your .qmd. Run each cell in order.

Note that this checks its work against existing data sources.

Read through backend/build/zoning/build.py.

What is the relationship of this to the .qmd we just looked at?
What are the final names of the tables it produces? How are these names produced?

Read through backend/query/core_functions.py. Take notes and write down questions.

What does sql_filter_block do? What functions help it do that? Walk yourself through the logic in detail, and explain why it might be useful with reference to the data engineering concepts from part (2).

Read through backend/query/zoning.py.

Take notes and write down questions.
How does this file read in sql into its functions? Where is that sql stored?
Can you think of a way to reduce reused code on this page?

Find and look at the zoning code in the backend/api folder as well. Explain how they work. How does the frontend find what filters a zoning query needs? Why isn’t there anything in the schema about the fourth table build in table_build.qmd?
Reiterate the general data engineering philosophy and work from this section, and reflect. Some suggestions:

Are there any areas you noticed that don’t fit with the Tidy philosophy?
Anything that seemed unclear or that could use improvement?
What was the most interesting or striking thing you learned?




Getting to Work
Your project is to take a new dataset and move from the old way of accessing data to a new one. Look through the datasets in backend/Data. Pick one that you are interested in and message me, who will assign you an github issue to complete the following project, with a Pull Request created after each step.

revamp the data collection process, if possible.
port functionality in app_utils over to sql and duckdb.

create a similar table_build.qmd page for your dataset, walking through how you built the tables and what decisions were involved. You should include more comments and discussion than in the previous one, and show that you’ve played around with the data enough that your decisions are grounded in it. Keep your notebook clear and organized with “##” section headers and so on.

discuss with me any decision to split the dataset into different tables than previously. This is probably a good idea, but we should talk about it.

create a similar build.py page for your dataset, consolidated down from the table_build.

Use the .sql datasets you’ve used to construct a similar dataset overview and basic analysis (with plots, tables, etc.) in a quarto notebook similar to introductory project. Put the dataset in that project, render the notebook there, and send a link to me.
Update logic to reference sql tables:

create a similar dataset.py query page for your dataset.
refigure and reconstruct the fastapi calls to make reference to the sql queries you built, just as in the zoning api calls.
add filtering/joining information to the schema.json. For now, the primary dataset will almost certainly just be “default”.
HARD OPTIONAL BONUS : these updates will probably break the frontend. If you’ve been working on your typescript, you can try to fix it yourself, or just let me know and I’ll fix it.

NOTE: if you don’t fix it yourself, don’t make a pull request, just notify me.

title: Introduction
text:
This mini-website will serve as an introduction to the skills and projects we’ll be working on during the summer of 2026 for the Okemo Verso Pod.



Git is really great for working on projects together as well as for storing your stuff cheaply. Hopefully VERSO’s main onboarding helped with that.
Quarto Notebooks (.qmd) give you the advantages of jupyter notebooks in a more replicable and git-friendly way:

Incredibly versatile, and can include any Python code as well as R.
Interactive coding environment
One document sources converts to:

Interactive slides
.html for websites, just like this one
.ipynb jupyter notebook files
.pdf files. Note this can use Latex, like: \(2 = \frac{10}{5}\)

Are purely text-based, so git differentials make sense and are actually readable.

Coding practices

Using a project-wide formatter. We’ll use ruff.

Keeps code readable and short
Minimizes unnecessary git differentials.

Proper git usage

commit on every meaningful change
pull request every complete feature.
respond to, and fix, reviews.

Type hints

clearer code
easier bug hunts


Data Engineering for larger-scale data-science

ETL
See how data works when you have a lot of it that you want to use at different times, many times, in different ways.

Policy Research

Building good projects often means translating prior work or uncertain requests. This will help with that.

Typescript (Optional)

learn true power of types
learn how internet actually works






Benefits Cliff

Languages: qmd files (no code) and typescript logic
Goal: help legislators and everyday people understand:

what benefits are available
how those benefits change with income or family situation
how those benefits relate with census information about income and family situation

Work to be done:

Adding more benefits

Policy review: build out core logic in qmd files for calculating benefits from policy manuals and other resources
typescript: code up algorithms
backfill: work through existing typescript algorithms and backfill the logic into qmd documentation.

Part 2: Extension

Add in information about resources required for life per county
Data analysis: pull in census information, etc., and see how comparisons work out.



Vermont Reports

Languages: SQL (duckdb), qmd, and Python.
Goal: help citizens, select boards, local government, and planners better understand their towns
Work to be done:

Data Engineering:

Updating all data engineering logic :

get data (external APIs or raw download)
build clean data (SQL and python scripts)

requires lots of though and consultation about how we should most effectively split up the tables.

runtime queries / logic (SQL and python scripts)
api (pythons’ FASTAPI library)
frontend

Removing and cleaning legacy code

Analysis:

Adding in new functionality and places for analysis, especially putting different data streams in conversation with each other

EG, how broadband and wastewater infrastructure inter-relate.




TBD:

Languages: almost certainly SQL, Python, .qmd
Goal: help people of Vermont. Working with Kendall to see exactly what that is.

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
The point of this project is to get some basic familiarity with qmd files, duckdb, and SQL if you don’t already have any.
Please complete this project in order. Spend no more than 12-15 hours on it unless you’re having a blast or answering questions that are really interesting to you. You’re getting paid to learn something!



Remember: the point is learning and ownership. This project is not for a grade, it’s for you to get ready for the summer, learn a lot, have fun, and hopefully build a resume. You’ll get paid either way, so make the time worth something to yourself.
DO NOT copy and paste anything from AI, or use any AI learning tool directly.
FEEL FREE to ask AI any questions, carefully read its answers, including reading functions that it wrote, and then reimplement them, or the logic behind them, in your code.
Have fun!

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
0: Repo Setup

Create a github repository named [your_name]-okemo-data.
Make the repo public, and share it with me.
Add a README, explaining what the project is, if you haven’t already, and commit it.

For all future steps, git commit at the end of every step where it makes sense. Include a message saying what you’ve done. At the end of each section, git rebase and squash, add, and push. Ask an LLM about what rebase is and why it’s useful.

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
1: Code setup
Note, all of the below is operating system sensitive. Feel free to ask AI to help you with it – but do the steps yourself, and pay attention to what’s going on!

Get a package manager of some sort: conda or uv.
Create a python environment with duckdb in it. Add whatever else you need when you need it.
Download quarto and get it connected to your terminal.
If you don’t already, get an IDE code editor (VS code, X Code, Sublime, etc.)

If you’re married to VIM, or whatever, that’s okay, so long as it doesn’t disrupt your work. Note that vscode has a VIM method.

Add ruff. It won’t work in quarto, but you need to do it sometime.

install it if you haven’t already
add a .toml with your ruff specifications
Add a separate playground

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
2: Data Engineering

Get a dataset from kaggle or somewhere like it.
Create a Data folder and store the data in there. Make sure you specify that it is raw.
Create a folder for your .qmd files and create an engineering.qmd file in it.
Create a yaml header for your Quarto document. Look at the code in this repository for some ideas.
Start coding! Begin by moving to the root and importing with code like this:


import os
from pathlib import Path
import duckdb

_project_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_project_root / ".git").exists():
    _project_root = _project_root.parent
    if _project_root == _project_root.parent:
        raise RuntimeError(".git not found — are you inside the repo?")
os.chdir(_project_root)
print(os.getcwd())

/home/fitsl/workbench/verso_okemo_onboarding


Write, in plain text, what this code does, above it. Do this for all future cells. You don’t have to go super detailed. Explain like I’m curious but not technical. Note that the code in this is turned off due to the yaml piece at the beginning (see the code for details).
If this code doesn’t make sense you or doesn’t work, just use os.chdir("dir") to your repo root. Note that code can hang on the above, so if things are taking a long time, that’s a likely culprit.

Get the dataset into memory using pandas.
Do the same using duckdb. You will have to use code that looks something like:


from pathlib import Path

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute(f"""

Note that the code instead the strings con.execute(" ") is sql. If you don’t know any sql, watch a youtube video, or ask an AI, or whatever helps you learn. It’s designed to be readable, but it can still be tricky sometimes. SQL keywords are generally in all-caps, and table/var names are in lower-case.

Using both pandas and SQL, show that you know how to examine the data:

get the names of the columns (hint, use SQLs “DESCRIBE”)
get the unique value counts for one or two of the columns
clean or reformat the data in some way. If nothing jumps out to you that can be cleaned, just doing something random (split columns, add a dummy variable, pivot form long to wide, etc.)
discuss your general sense of the data
make a few basic plots using matplotlib or seaborn. Nothing fancy, and very low level and summarizing.


Remember to articulate before each cell block what you want and expect it to do. If you’re better at one language or the other, do that first and then work from that as an example.

Split the data into separate .parquet files by first creating views or tables using some portions of the columns, then save those views to parquet files. Make sure you don’t overwrite your existing data files; these are your clean tables. Use easily parseable names.

What’s the meaningful difference between an SQL view and a table? Why would we want one or the other? Put your answer in plain text in your qmd.

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
3. Data Analysis and Report

Create a new report.qmd file with the same initial structure (yaml, root, imports) as engineering.qmd.
Make a db connection to your three parquet files. Name them after what you parse in.
Now you get to actually ask some questions of your data. Pick two or three things you’re genuinely curious about. Before each cell, write in plain text what question you’re asking and what you expect to find. Then write code to answer it, getting the data both with pandas and with SQL. Note if there are any places that one or the other seems more or less difficult. Some ideas:

group by a category and compare averages, counts, or sums across groups
filter down to an interesting subset and see how it differs from the whole


Example to see the number of rows for each value in a column District_Name:

df = con.execute("""--sql
  SELECT 
    District_Name as District,
    COUNT(*) AS Count,
  FROM zoning 
  GROUP BY District_Name
  ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC
  LIMIT 15
""").df()

Make a few plots that tell a story. Use matplotlib or seaborn. Aim for 2-4 plots that each make a point. For each one:

say in plain text what the plot is meant to show before you make it
give it a real title, axis labels, and legend
write a sentence or two after it on what you actually see, and whether it matched what you expected


Example plot to visualize the above:

import seaborn as sns 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt 

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=df, x="District", y="Count", hue="District", ax=ax, palette="tab20", legend=True)
plt.title("Top Zoning District Types in Vermont")
ax.set_xticks([])
plt.legend(loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.05), ncol=3)
plt.show()









Write a short conclusion. What did you learn about the data? What would you look at next if you had more time? What surprised you? No need to dazzle here, just be honest and clearly communicative.

title: Onboarding Data Project
text:
4. Publish
The goal is a small github.io website with your rendered .qmd pages, plus a downloadable pdf of your report.

Add a _quarto.yml project file at the root that builds a website. Look at Quarto’s website docs – you want a project: type: website and a navbar linking your engineering.qmd and report.qmd pages. Ask AI to explain any field you don’t recognize, then write it yourself. See the _quarto_yml in this repo if you get stuck.
Configure your report.qmd to also render to pdf. You’ll add format: with both html and pdf to its yaml header. You may need a LaTeX install – quarto install tinytex is the easy path. Add a link on your site so people can download the pdf. If this proves impossible, that’s also fine.
Render the whole site locally with quarto render and open it in your browser. Fix anything that looks broken. Make sure code, plots, and the pdf link all work.
Publish to GitHub Pages. The simplest way is to go to settings in github browser, then pages, then deploy from a branch. Read what it prints; it’ll tell you your https://[your_name].github.io/[your_name]-okemo-data URL.
Put that live URL at the top of your repo’s README, and share it with me.
